author: Times Leader Editorial Board
title: Editorial: Data center regulation is ever-evolving - NewsBreak
text:
By Times Leader Editorial Board ,
17 hours ago Commonwealth Media Services Recurring talk of “moratoriums” and other outright blocking of data center construction tend to ignore a simple reality: Like it or not, tremendous amounts of money are flowing into the growth of artificial intelligence, and until the companies behind it figure out how to provide greater AI abilities with less computer power and energy demands, we will see data centers cropping up anywhere they can build them, regardless of what we do in our state, county or municipality.
Put another way, for all practical purposes, data centers have become a fungible resource. Their output reaches customers through the ubiquitous internet, so it doesn’t really matter where companies build them. The goal increasingly should not be to stop them, but to control where they are placed and how they impact energy, water, the environment and residential areas.
Controlling such factors has historic resonance in our region, which prospered with the growth of King Coal only to endure its lasting, ugly legacy of mine-scarred lands, sinkholes emerging where abandoned tunnels collapse, and acid mine drainage turning our waterways a lethal orange.
The question is less about whether data centers will be built and more about whether the owners act responsibly once they are constructed, paying for any impacts both while they operate and after they become obsolete.
To that end, we think that Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s executive order issuing tighter controls over data center construction statewide is a pretty solid first step, at least upon first look.
The woman challenging Shapiro for his job this fall, Republican State Treasurer Stacy Garrity, rightly pointed out that Shapiro is shifting his stance , noting he previously embraced data center development and has accepted campaign donations from “data center interests.” But we think she goes a bit too far trying to paint the new EO efforts as a convenient shift with the political winds.
The data center industry is exploding in ways few outside the frontier of technology predicted. Seeing governors and other politicians react to the rapid changes with more restrictions and elimination of tax exemptions (a suspect strategy from the start) can just as easily be seen as a valid response to those changes and to constituent concerns. Garrity and other Shapiro critics would be better off proposing their own, detailed solutions to the evolving tech landscape.
Shapiro’s plan requires much more scrutiny both during and after implementation. It must remain a work in progress that can be adapted as the tech and economic factors invariably change. It would be better if more of it were written into law rather than issued through executive order. And of course, many of the steps it proposes would work best in a world where other states competing for the boon data centers promise to implement similar restrictions.
But even with all those caveats, it looks like a good, fairly comprehensive effort to rein in some of the more suspect issues from the data center boom, while providing a higher degree of local control over the placement and impact of the facilities.
